catalog_quote: TT is a tonal language. Syllables have H[igh], L[ow], F[alling], or R[ising] tone. F is the same as <HL>, and R is equivalent to <LH>, where angled brackets indicate syllabic groupings. ... In addition to lexical tones on noun, verb, and other stems, there are some word-internal grammatical tone overlays, and other overlays affecting words that are controlled by the morphosyntactic context. As a result, the lexical tones are often completely overwritten ... [3.7.1] Each noun, adjective, numeral, verb, and other lexical stem has a lexical tone contour. These lexical tones may be overridden by superimposed stem-wide tone contours required by the inflectional morphology (in the case of verbs) or by the syntax (in the case of nouns and other NP components). Unpublished cross-Dogon typology manuscript, Dogon and Bangime Linguistics (Moran, Forkel & Heath eds., MPI-EVA), DLP Document; PDF, 677 KB.https://dogonlanguages.info/sources/dogonlexicaltonesofstems
tone_statements.quote: In eastern Dogon languages, the typical situation is that verbs are either lexically /H/ or /LH/. … In Toro Tegu, the chaining form brings out lexical tone melodies, but must be supplemented by another form such as the imperative that express the full lexical vocalism. For example, ‘go up’ has chaining form ùnú, which shows the /LH/ melody … In Toro Tegu, all Cv stems are basically /H/-toned Cv́. … typical lexical melodies for uncompounded stems other than verbs are /H/, /HL/, /LH/, and /LHL/. … there are several /HLH/ nouns in Toro Tegu, e.. kâ:nú ‘monkey’.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 1 ('verbs: primary lexical melodies'), 3 ('verbs: distinguishing lexical melodies from grammatical tone overlays'), 4 ('verbs: tones of monomoraic Cv'), 5 ('nouns, adjectives, numerals')
tone_statements.summary: Lexical H/L tone melodies on stems: Toro Tegu verbs /H/ or /LH/ (trisyllabic L.L.H), Cv verbs /H/, 'bring' /HLH/; nouns /H/ /HL/ /LH/ /LHL/ plus /HLH/; grammatical overlays erase lexical melodies.

Unpublished cross-Dogon typology manuscript (uses the older name Tabi-Sarinyere for Toro Tegu), Dogon and Bangime Linguistics (MPI-EVA), DLP Document; MS Word.doc, 50 KB.https://dogonlanguages.info/sources/dogonlexicaltonesofverbsandotherstemclasses
tone_statements.quote: Notation: curly brackets {...} indicate the sequence of distinct tones (from one to three) in the tone contour … Angled brackets <...> indicate the tone contour of a specific syllable if this contour is not simple L[ow] or H[igh]. … With few exceptions there is a lexical choice between two contours: {H} [all-high-toned] {LH} [rising contour] … In one set of languages, the tone break occurs as close as possible to the right edge of the stem, so the H-tone appears only on the final mora and all preceding moras are low-toned. … This is the case in Jamsay, Beni, and Tabi-Sarinyere.
tone_statements.locator: unpaginated (no page breaks); intro 'Notation' paragraph + section 'verbs (vowel-final, bimoraic or longer)'
tone_statements.summary: Stems carry lexical tone contours of H and L: verbs {H} or {LH} (H on the final mora in Tabi-Sarinyere), rare {HLH} zeeri 'bring'; nouns {H},{HL},{LH},{LHL},{HLH}; every stem needs an H tone.

tone_statements.citation: McPherson, Laura. 2014. Replacive grammatical tone in the Dogon languages. PhD dissertation, University of California, Los Angeles. eScholarship permalinkhttps://escholarship.org/uc/item/7hh0k529;open PDFs at linguistics.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/ and bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.dartmouth.edu/dist/5/444/files/2020/10/
tone_statements.quote: There are two phonemic tones, H and L, marked with acute (v́) and grave (v̀) accents, respectively; unmarked syllables are toneless. … 3.3.5 Toro Tegu … In Toro Tegu, core NP possessors assign {L} to the possessed noun while complex NP possessors assign {HL}: (38) a. ànú L ı̀lò (Toro Tegu) man house ‘a man’s house’ (/ı́ló/) b. [ànùL Nú] HL ı́lò (Toro Tegu) man this house ‘this man’s house’ As we can see, this choice between {L} and {HL} has nothing to do with the phonology of the syllable immediately preceding the possessed noun: both are H-toned Nú.
tone_statements.locator: p. 2 fn. 1 and p. 169 sec. 3.3.5 'Toro Tegu'
tone_statements.summary: Two phonemic tones, H and L (stated for Dogon generally); in Toro Tegu lexical word tones are replaced by grammatical overlays, {L} after simple possessors and {HL} after complex or pronominal ones.

tone_statements.citation: Heath, Jeffrey. n.d. Dogon: syntactic tonology of NP [document heading: 'Dogon syntactic tonology of NP']. Unpublished cross-Dogon typology manuscript (uses the older name Tabi-Sarinyere for Toro Tegu; predecessor of 'Dogon tonosyntax of NP' 2014), Dogon and Bangime Linguistics (MPI-EVA), DLP Document; MS Word.doc, 39 KB.https://dogonlanguages.info/sources/dogonsyntactictonologyofnp
tone_statements.quote: Tonal processes are critical in the grammatical systems of Dogon languages. It is necessary to recognize three ontologically distinct types of tones: … lexical tones … floating-tone morphemes … stem-level tone-contour overlays … lexical tones may be of the general form {H}, {HL}, {LH}, {LHL}, and in some languages also {HLH}, but not {L}. … the prenominal possessor imposes either {L} or {HL} contour on the possessed NP … mix of {HL} and {L}: Beni, Nanga, Tabi-Sarinyere … final L-tone requires {L} on the possessed noun while final H-tone requires {HL}.
tone_statements.locator: unpaginated; opening paragraphs (types of tones, notation, lexical contours) + possessor-overlay table and following paragraph naming Tabi-Sarinyere
tone_statements.summary: Dogon-wide: lexical tone built from H and L (stem melodies {H},{HL},{LH},{LHL}), floating tones, grammatical {L}/{HL} overlays; Toro Tegu (Tabi-Sarinyere) has possessor-conditioned {HL}/{L} overlays.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim in the held 2010 draft at the stated sections. The deciding source is the language's only reference grammar, by its fieldworker; Glottolog's three descriptive refs are all versions of it. The 2015 published edition (open, CC-BY) was downloaded and read at the same sections: it restates that TT is a tonal language with syllabic H/L/<HL>/<LH> tones, lexical stem melodies (all-L excluded) and grammatical/tonosyntactic overlays, with the only rhythmic material being the morphologically conditioned strong/weak vowel-reduction grid in verb stems (sec. 3.2.2), explicitly not a stress system. Classification 'tonal, no word stress described' stands. Only action: re-point the citation/locator to Heath 2015 (DOI 10.17617/2.2157088, pp. 5, 15-16, 54-55) instead of the the Internet Archive 2010 draft; no reclassification. Caveat: web search for independent prosody/instrumental studies could not be run

sources.quote: 'TT is a tonal language. Syllables have H[igh], L[ow], falling <HL>, or rising <LH> tone. ... In addition to lexical tones on noun, verb, and other stems, there are some word-internal grammatical tone overlays, and other overlays affecting words that are controlled by the morphosyntactic context.' Sec. 3.7.1: 'Each noun, adjective, numeral, verb, or other stem has a lexical tone melody. ... The one theoretically possible tone pattern that is excluded as a possible lexical melody is all-low /L/. That is, every stem has at least one H-tone component.'
